answer: `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]` sets the limit on that one port instance; direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all), location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all), and the thresholds are uint64/int64/decimal64 or na/not-supported (default na). `set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` does the same per resource type and its show adds default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. The crossing is only reported if `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true` (with data-supervision true) is set; pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision decides that for newly created resources. `show pm-parameter-errored-seconds` gives the parameter's units and type. The raised TCA is read with `show alarm`.

Enable protocol and authentication: `set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true` (defaults ntp-enabled true, ntp-auth-enabled false, assignment-method both, from manual, dhcp, both). Create the key: `add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]`, key-id 1..65534, key-type sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value 8..40 characters, is-trusted default false, e.g. `add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera`. Bind it: `add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>`; the address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS name, origin manual (default) or dhcp, admin-state default unlock. Check with `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>`: auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means all recent probes answered), stratum, poll, delay, offset, jitter, condition. `show ntp ntp-active-server` names the server in use and `show clock time-source` should read ntp.

Traffic is moved with `protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>`, Operational mode only. operation-type is force, lockout, manual or release; switch-target is not needed for release and lockout. Example: `protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection`. The controller is moved with `manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>`, where resource is the AID of the object to switch, e.g. `manual-switchover card-1-3` on a G42, `card-1-5` on a G32, `card-1-12` on a G34c; it prompts 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. A persistent switch request can also be configured with `set protection-group-<name> pg-request`: clear (default), manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout, exercise (bidirectional SNCP only).

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an active NTP synchronisation is what rejects your manual setting. Run `show clock` and read time-source (ntp or manual, default manual), current-time, universal-time, timezone (default Universal-Time-Coordinated), DST-active and last-time-jump, which is reported as '<time1> to <time2>' and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. Then `show ntp` for ntp-enabled (default true), ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server and assignment-method, and `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>` for reach, stratum, offset, jitter, auth-status and condition. If you do want manual time, disable NTP first and use the ISO 8601 form: `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z`, or with an offset, `set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00`. The `time` command reports current time in the system configured timezone.

`show ne` identifies the node: ne-id, ne-name (default '1830 GX'), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-vendor, ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), contact, equipment-discovery-ready and recover-mode. `status` (or `status system`) is a dashboard of NE properties, SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity and equipment counts; `status equipment [<chassis-id>]` lists chassis, cards and toms. Contents also come from `show equipment`, `show slot` (supported-type, installed-type, current-equipment) and `show inventory`. The cost: `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]`. With no resource-id it restarts the active controller card; type defaults to warm. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, warm reboots the processor and is non service affecting, shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Connectivity returns within five minutes. Sub-components are listed with `show card resources`.

Slot 2 of chassis 1 is `slot-1-2` (`slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`, showing AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state, current-equipment). The card fitted there is `card-1-2`. Off the card hang `port-1-2-<port-name>` (`port-<card-name>-<port-name>`), and under each port the function object: `comm-eth-1-2-<port>`, `usb-1-2-<port>`, or the pluggable `tom-1-2-<port>` (`tom-<card-name>-<port-name>`; adding a TOM auto-creates the tributary port termination point and deleting the TOM deletes it). Also under the card: `capabilities-1-2`, `sub-component-1-2/<name>`, `serdes-1-2-<port>/<serdes-name>`, `current-fw` and `led-<location>/<name>`. FRU inventory for the pluggable is `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. `show inventory-1-3-1`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

What a model can take: `show supported-card-<card-type>` gives node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw in W, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate), default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band) and supported-features. Related: `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>`, `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>`, `show tom-type-<tom-type>`. What the installed card is doing: `show card-<name>` with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, max-power-draw, power-profile, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, parent-card, subcard-list, admin-state (default unlock), oper-state and avail-state. `show capabilities-<name>` reports that card's own capabilities.

The stated chain is: `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version <ospfv2|ospfv3>] [router-id-mode <manual|use-loopback>]`, instance-id 0..255, version default ospfv2, router-id-mode default use-loopback - and with use-loopback the ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. Then `add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>` (type normal); the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Then `add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>`; the instance and area must be present, and ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface if-name. Defaults: enable true, hello-interval 10 (1..32767 s), router-dead-interval 40 (4..65535 s), retransmission-interval 5, transmit-delay 1, ospf-cost 10, priority 1, ospf-if-routing auto. Progress: `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id>`, state down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. Its pre-condition is that the neighbor NEs also have instance, area and interface configured and are properly connected with DCN interface bridges; the neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Per controller card use `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, e.g. `show software-load-1-5/active`. It returns swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed, timeout), swload-information, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. Individual pieces: `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version and description, and one level deeper `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. Firmware bundled with that load: `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`; versions of the same firmware can differ per equipment-type.

Per port and direction, `show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress`: total-frames-out counts LLDP frames transmitted through the port, total-frames-in counts frames received, plus error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs and total-ageouts (all default 0), last-change-time and last-clear-time. The egress direction is not supported, and all counters for a port freeze whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled on that port. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress` shows what was actually discovered: chassis-id and chassis-id-subtype, port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, capabilities, age, last-update, ttl; the information is kept until the port is decommissioned or manually cleared. `show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>` shows what we advertise, where chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, port-description the port name and system-name the NE name. Global `show lldp hold-on-timer` (default 900 seconds) applies when a neighbor sends no TTL TLV.

`show slot`, or `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` / `show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>`, lists every holder with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; an unpopulated position shows a supported-type but an empty installed-type and current-equipment '---'. FRU detail is `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`: hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable). Firmware level is `show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>` giving fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable), e.g. current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 against expected 0x28 is not-current. Equipment detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller is under `show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>`.

`show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` lists the downloaded manifests; manifest-signature is a hex string up to 1024 characters and downloaded-on a YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ timestamp. Contents are `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown) - that is the per-piece install result. Firmware carried in the package is `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`, and packaged FRU data per equipment type is `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>`. To compare with what is actually on the node, use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` and `show sw-subcomponent-...` (same installed / not-installed / installation-failed / unknown states) and `show packaged-fw`; installation progress across versions is `show upgrade-status`.

Alarm severity defaults come from the alarm-severity-profile, a system-managed object that cannot be manually deleted: `set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>` and `show alarm-severity-profile`. The individual entry is `alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>`, direction na, ingress or egress and location na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Examples: `set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor`, `set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major`. PM defaults come from the equally system-managed pm-profile: `set pm-profile global-data-supervision <auto-enabled|manual>` (default manual, meaning the flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or per pm-control-entry), and `set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision <true|false>] [default-tca-supervision <true|false>]`, which say whether newly created resources of that type get PM data supervision and threshold crossing supervision automatically enabled.

The deciding object is `ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>`; its `action` gives the IPsec treatment of the datagrams: protect, bypass or discard, default protect. It also carries mandatory `priority` (uint8, giving precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel (default) or transport, esn default true, anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 (used when action is protect), dynamic-ts default disabled and alarm-report-control default allowed. Underneath hangs `ipsec-traffic-selector-<local-instance>/<peer>/<spd-entry>/<ts-name>` with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or 0-255; default any), and under each traffic selector hang `local-subnet` and `remote-subnet` .../<prefix>, and `local-ports` and `remote-ports` .../<start>/<stop>, where start is all, opaque or a port number and stop defaults to 0 (only accepted when start is all or opaque). SPD entries for a peer are grouped by `security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>`.

`trusted-certificate-<id>` is the X509v3 CA certificate, root and intermediate, trusted by the system - the trust anchor that trust-chain leafrefs point at. `local-certificate-<id>` is this node's own identity, the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; it uniquely adds self-signed, used-by (secure-applications, ikev2-peers presently using it) and subject-alternative-names. `peer-certificate-<id>` is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, uniquely adding white-listed, true when it has no trust chain and was explicitly white-listed at import. All three are set/show only and share version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/3072/4096, ecdsa256/384/521), certificate-bytes in PEM, revocation-mode (auto default, force-revoked, force-unrevoked), alarm-report-control (default allowed) and label. The fourth is the plain `certificate` command: `show certificates`, `show certificate-revocation`, `clear certificate`.

Material arrives with `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`, Operational mode, importing one or more certificates in PEM format. The type is local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate, e.g. `import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <string in PEM format>`. -i additionally imports intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle, or those referenced through the AIA extension for a single-certificate file; root certificates must be installed individually. With no certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix (for /CN=Nokia: trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, -2). The passphrase decodes encrypted trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundle input. Removal is `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<id>`; the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type, and <tab> lists clearable ids. Bulk types: purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused, purge-peer-unused.

`access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name>` holds the decision: its mandatory `action` is permit or deny, applied when the filters match - path (default *), module-name (default *), attribute and attribute-value (leaf-lists, max 10 entries of 64 characters) and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *). `access-rule-list-<name>` groups rules by user-group and holds the ordering: the list is processed in order as given by sequence-id, lower ids first. Both govern management access to YANG data nodes, RPCs, notifications and other non-YANG commands, not forwarded traffic. Packet filtering is `acl-<name>` (type IPv4 or IPv6, bound to an interface such as 1-AUX-1, DCN, DCN-B) with `ace-<name>/<sequence-id>` entries whose action is drop (default), accept or reject. The object with nothing to do with traffic at all is `sw-control-rule-<service-name>`: it overrides the action on software service failure, fail-action being default-action, ignore or system-restart.

Rules are processed in sequence-id order, lower number ids first, so of two matching rules the lower sequence-id takes effect; this applies both to access-rule entries within a list and to access-rule-list objects, since the access-rule-list is processed in the order given by sequence-id. If sequence-id (uint16) is not provided on add, it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the entry goes to the end of the list; the id can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On `access-rule-list-<name>` the `user-group` attribute is a leaf-list of user-group names with a maximum of 20 user-groups referenced; its default value '*' is the match-all representation, meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists, and every access-rule must be given an action of permit or deny when it is created.

The trap community string is not in snmp-community: the guide states the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`, or on an existing target with `set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>`. trap-community-string is a string of 0..32 characters, default 'infinera'; snmp-version defaults to v2c (v2c or v3, snmpv3-user only applies for v3), target-port defaults to 162 (range 0..65535), target-transport is udp, enabled defaults to true. `snmp-community-<name>` with community-string (1..32 characters) and community-string-access read-only governs polling access only; the global agent is `set snmp [enabled <true|false>] [port <1..65535>]`, defaults true and 161. Verify with `show snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string`.

`external-fiber-connection` is the one filled in by something other than you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations: `add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]`, scope being general-purpose (default) or cable-id and fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way). Only entries with scope cable-id are included in the CableID path and verified. The one you write yourself is `fiber-connection-<name>`, the physical link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE in an OADM/ILA topology, with src-port, dst-port and fiber-connection-type (default two-way). `show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> fiber-connection-list` shows the supporting path.

To give the node an address use `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, e.g. `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0` or `add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'`; show returns netmask and origin (static default, dhcp, auto-config). The interface itself is `interface-<if-name>`, with ipv4-enabled default true and ipv4-address-assignment-method static (default) or dhcp. The two look-alikes are read-only LLDP objects reporting advertised management addresses, not configuration: `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]` gives the management address received from the remote system on that port and direction, and `show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>` the same for the local LLDP ports. if-subtype takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. Neither assigns an address to an interface.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check the interface first: `show interface-<if-name>`, and set ipv4-address-assignment-method to static (values static, dhcp; default static) with ipv4-enabled true before adding. The other refusals are value validation: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) and 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are allowed to be configured. To see which interfaces are available, use '?' after the command `ipv4-address-` and the system displays the object completion options; `show interface` lists them with if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, backup-port, vrf, protection-mode, admin-state and oper-state. The syntax is `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`; `delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>` removes it.

Everything in use is under `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]`, which lists system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static routes; source-protocol names the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop is none (default), blackhole or unreachable. The tables are `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`, address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, with one system-controlled default RIB per routing instance per supported address family. Resolved next hops are `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]`, e.g. `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Hand-typed routes are added with `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label] [special-next-hop <value>]`; distance 1..255 default 1, advertised default false, origin manual (default) or dhcp. `ipv6-static-route` is the IPv6 equivalent.

`local-ports` and `remote-ports` belong to the management IPsec/IKEv2 tunnel. Both are keyed `<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>` and sit under an ipsec-traffic-selector inside an ipsec-spd-entry. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port number defaulting to 0, and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`, `add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all`, `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49`. `connection-ports` is the connectivity one: `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]` maps a degree (uint16, range 1..20) to the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card, e.g. connection-ports-1/1 to port-1-3-dwdm-line1. index is always 1 in 1830 GX since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional, and the OMS of the corresponding dwdm port is created as a consequence.

The copy is made with `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, Operational mode, storing the current state of the Configuration database into one of the available backup slots. db-instance is temp (default, used for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage), the automatic onehour, oneday, oneweek, or rollback; description is up to 128 characters. It is refused unless db-passphrase is configured, either globally as part of security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or given on the command; the passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic snapshots stay disabled until it is set, and re-taking an existing instance such as oneweek overwrites the file. Restore with `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]` (default false); pre-condition, a snapshot must have been taken. List them with `show database` or `show database-<database-type>`.
